about: Curated, educational index of documents that governments once kept secret and have since released officially. Each entry points to the archive that holds the original and to a search of that archive; nothing here is leaked or restricted material.

cia.name: Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) Electronic Reading Room
cia.holds: About 13 million pages, including the CIA Records Search Tool (CREST) collection of 25-year-old records released under Executive Order 13526.

nara.name: U.S. National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) Catalog
nara.holds: Federal records, including those released by the National Declassification Center.

jfk.name: NARA: President John F. Kennedy Assassination Records Collection
jfk.holds: Over 5 million pages gathered under the JFK Records Act of 1992, with releases from 2017 to 2025.

fbi.name: Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Records: The Vault
fbi.holds: Files the FBI has released under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA).

nsa.name: National Security Agency (NSA) declassification and historical releases
nsa.holds: Historical cryptologic releases such as Venona and the Gulf of Tonkin signals intelligence.

nsarchive.name: National Security Archive at George Washington University
nsarchive.holds: An independent non-governmental research institute that obtains records through FOIA and publishes them in electronic briefing books.

wilson.name: Wilson Center Digital Archive: International History Declassified
wilson.holds: Translated records from the archives of former communist states and many other countries.

uk.name: The National Archives (United Kingdom): Discovery catalogue
uk.holds: Government records released under the Public Records Act, including Security Service (MI5) and Government Code and Cypher School files.

stasi.name: Stasi Records Archive (German Federal Archives)
stasi.holds: About 111 km of files kept by East Germany's Ministry for State Security, open to the people they concern and to researchers.

lac.name: Library and Archives Canada (LAC)
lac.holds: Federal government records, including security and intelligence files.

india.name: Abhilekh Patal: National Archives of India portal
india.holds: Digitised Government of India records, including the files on Subhas Chandra Bose released from 2016.

jacar.name: Japan Center for Asian Historical Records (JACAR)
jacar.holds: Digitised records from Japan's National Archives, Diplomatic Archives and Ministry of Defense up to 1945.

brazil.name: Arquivo Nacional (National Archives of Brazil)
brazil.holds: Records of the 1964–1985 military dictatorship, released through the Memórias Reveladas project.

churchill.name: Churchill Archives Centre, University of Cambridge
churchill.holds: Papers of Winston Churchill and others, and the Mitrokhin Archive of KGB notes.

ia.name: Internet Archive
ia.holds: A non-profit library with many public copies of released government documents.

blackvault.name: The Black Vault
blackvault.holds: A private collection of millions of pages obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests.

muckrock.name: MuckRock
muckrock.holds: A non-profit newsroom where anyone can file public-records requests and read the responses.

docs.title: Zimmermann Telegram
docs.by: German Foreign Office (intercepted by British naval intelligence)
docs.summary: A coded German proposal that Mexico join the war against the United States. British codebreakers in Room 40 decrypted it; its publication helped bring the United States into the First World War.

docs.title: Operation Mincemeat files
docs.summary: A corpse carrying fake invasion plans was floated ashore in Spain to convince Germany the Allies would land in Greece rather than Sicily. The full files were opened at the UK National Archives in 1996.

docs.title: Ultra: the Bletchley Park codebreaking records
docs.summary: Intelligence from breaking the German Enigma and Lorenz ciphers. The secret was kept until 1974; Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ) records went to the National Archives in the HW series from the 1990s.

docs.title: Wannsee Conference protocol
docs.summary: Minutes of the meeting that coordinated the Nazi plan to murder the Jews of Europe. The only surviving copy was found in German Foreign Office files in 1947 and used at the Nuremberg trials.

docs.title: Katyn massacre: Soviet 'Package No. 1'
docs.by: Politburo of the Soviet Communist Party
docs.summary: The Politburo order to shoot about 22,000 Polish officers and others. The Soviet Union blamed Nazi Germany for decades; Russia handed the sealed file to Poland in 1992.

docs.title: MAGIC intercepts before Pearl Harbor
docs.by: U.S. Army Signal Intelligence Service and Navy OP-20-G
docs.summary: Decrypted Japanese diplomatic messages (the 'Purple' cipher) read in the weeks before the attack. They were examined in public by the Congressional inquiry of 1945–1946.

docs.title: Trinity test reports, Manhattan Project
docs.summary: The first nuclear explosion. Parts of the story were published in the Smyth Report in August 1945; most technical records were declassified over the following decades.

docs.title: Operation Paperclip records
docs.summary: The programme that brought German scientists, including the V-2 rocket team, to the United States. Many records were opened under the Nazi War Crimes Disclosure Act of 1998.

docs.title: Gouzenko defection papers
docs.by: Soviet embassy (documents carried out by Igor Gouzenko)
docs.summary: A Soviet cipher clerk walked out of the embassy with 109 documents on spy rings in Canada. The Kellock–Taschereau Royal Commission report followed in 1946; many files were opened later.

docs.title: The Long Telegram
docs.by: George F. Kennan, U.S. Department of State
docs.summary: Kennan's 5,000-word cable on Soviet behaviour, which shaped the policy of containment. It was classified when sent and published in the Foreign Relations of the United States series in 1969.

docs.title: Venona decrypts
docs.by: U.S. Army Signal Intelligence Service, later NSA
docs.summary: A 37-year effort to read Soviet intelligence messages sent in the 1940s. About 3,000 partial decryptions were released in 1995–1996 and named many Soviet sources in the West.

docs.title: NSC-68
docs.summary: A top secret policy paper that called for a large military build-up against the Soviet Union. It became the blueprint for Cold War policy and was declassified in 1975.

docs.title: Stalin–Kim Il Sung correspondence on Korea
docs.summary: Soviet records showing Stalin approving Kim Il Sung's plan to invade the South. Russia gave copies to South Korea in 1994 and the Wilson Center translated them.

docs.title: TPAJAX: the 1953 coup in Iran
docs.by: Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and British intelligence
docs.summary: The operation that overthrew Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh. The CIA formally acknowledged its role in records released in 2013, and more followed in 2017.

docs.title: PBSuccess: the 1954 coup in Guatemala
docs.summary: The covert operation against President Jacobo Árbenz. The CIA released about 1,400 pages in 1997, including a manual on assassination.

docs.title: MKUltra
docs.summary: Mind-control and drug experiments, some on people who did not consent. Most files were destroyed in 1973; about 20,000 surviving documents were found and released after a 1977 FOIA request.

docs.title: Soviet decisions on the Hungarian Revolution
docs.by: Presidium of the Soviet Communist Party
docs.summary: Notes of the Kremlin meetings that decided to crush the uprising. They were published after Soviet archives opened.

docs.title: Kyshtym nuclear disaster reports
docs.by: CIA analysis of a Soviet accident
docs.summary: A waste tank exploded at a secret Soviet plutonium plant. The Soviet Union admitted it only in 1989; CIA files on it were released through FOIA from 1977.

docs.title: U-2 history acknowledging Area 51
docs.summary: The CIA's history of the U-2 spy plane. A less redacted version obtained in 2013 was the first official acknowledgement of the Area 51 test site.

docs.title: Project Blue Book
docs.summary: The Air Force study of 12,618 reports of unidentified flying objects (1952–1969). The case files went to the National Archives in 1976.

docs.title: Official history of the Bay of Pigs operation
docs.summary: The CIA's own five-volume history of the failed invasion of Cuba. Volumes were released in 2011 and 2016 after a FOIA lawsuit.

docs.title: Tsar Bomba test film
docs.summary: The largest explosion ever made, about 50 megatons. Russia's nuclear agency released a 40-minute film of the test in 2020.

docs.title: Operation Northwoods
docs.summary: A proposal for staged attacks to justify war with Cuba. President Kennedy's administration rejected it; it was released in 1997 by the Assassination Records Review Board.

docs.title: Cuban Missile Crisis reconnaissance
docs.by: CIA and the National Photographic Interpretation Center
docs.summary: U-2 photographs of Soviet missile sites and the records of the Executive Committee (ExComm). Large releases came around the 30th anniversary in 1992.

docs.title: Kim Philby files
docs.summary: Records on the British intelligence officer who spied for the Soviet Union and fled from Beirut in 1963. MI5 files on the Cambridge spy ring have been released in the KV series.

docs.title: JFK assassination records
docs.by: FBI, CIA, Warren Commission and others
docs.summary: Records on the assassination of President Kennedy collected under the JFK Records Act of 1992. Most were released by 2017–2023; the remaining withheld files followed in 2025.

docs.title: Gulf of Tonkin signals intelligence
docs.summary: Intercepts used to report a second attack on U.S. destroyers, which led to the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution. An NSA history released in 2005 concluded that the second attack did not happen.

docs.title: U.S. embassy cables on Indonesia 1965–1966
docs.summary: Cables showing what U.S. officials knew of the mass killings of suspected communists. About 30,000 pages were declassified in 2017.

docs.title: Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia
docs.by: Soviet and Czechoslovak communist party records
docs.summary: Records of the decision to end the Prague Spring by force, published after 1989 from Czech and Russian archives.

docs.title: The Pentagon Papers
docs.by: Office of the Secretary of Defense
docs.summary: A secret history of U.S. decision-making in Vietnam from 1945 to 1967. Leaked in 1971; the full report was officially released in 2011.

docs.title: Chile Declassification Project
docs.by: CIA, State Department, White House and FBI
docs.summary: About 24,000 records on U.S. policy towards Chile before and after the coup that brought Augusto Pinochet to power, released in 1999–2000.

docs.title: The 'Family Jewels'
docs.summary: A 702-page internal list of CIA activities that may have broken the law, compiled in 1973. Released in 2007.

docs.title: Project Azorian
docs.summary: A secret attempt to raise a sunken Soviet submarine, K-129, with the ship Hughes Glomar Explorer. The CIA released its internal history in 2010.

docs.title: British nuclear tests at Maralinga
docs.summary: Records of nuclear tests on Aboriginal land, examined by the Royal Commission of 1984–1985 and opened in the National Archives of Australia.

docs.title: Archives of Terror (Operation Condor)
docs.summary: Police files found in a Paraguayan police station in 1992. They record Operation Condor, the cross-border campaign of South American dictatorships against their opponents.

docs.title: Argentina Declassification Project
docs.summary: About 50,000 pages on the military dictatorship of 1976–1983, handed to Argentina between 2016 and 2019 to help trace the disappeared.

docs.title: Stargate Project (remote viewing)
docs.summary: A long-running study of whether 'psychic' remote viewing could gather intelligence. It was ended and disclosed in 1995; the records are in the CIA Reading Room.

docs.title: Rendlesham Forest incident (UK UFO files)
docs.summary: Reports of lights near two U.S. Air Force bases. The Ministry of Defence released its UFO files to the National Archives between 2008 and 2013.

docs.title: Able Archer 83 and the 'Soviet War Scare'
docs.summary: A NATO nuclear exercise that Soviet leaders may have feared was cover for a real attack. A 1990 review called 'The Soviet War Scare' was declassified in 2015.

docs.title: KGB files on Chernobyl
docs.by: KGB of the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic
docs.summary: Reports on safety problems at the plant before and after the disaster. Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) archive released them, the latest set in 2021.

docs.title: British ambassador's Tiananmen cable
docs.summary: Ambassador Alan Donald's report on the killings around Tiananmen Square, opened at the National Archives in 2017.

docs.title: Stasi files
docs.by: Ministry for State Security of East Germany (Stasi)
docs.summary: Files on millions of people. Citizens occupied the Stasi offices to stop their destruction; since 1992 people can read their own file.

docs.title: Operation Gladio
docs.summary: Secret 'stay-behind' networks set up to resist a Soviet invasion. Prime Minister Giulio Andreotti revealed the Italian network to Parliament in 1990.

docs.title: The Mitrokhin Archive
docs.summary: Notes a KGB archivist copied secretly for years and brought to Britain in 1992. They were opened to the public at Cambridge in 2014.

docs.title: The 'genocide fax'
docs.by: United Nations Assistance Mission for Rwanda (UNAMIR)
docs.summary: General Roméo Dallaire's warning to UN headquarters of plans to exterminate Tutsi, three months before the genocide began.

docs.title: CORONA satellite imagery
docs.summary: The first American spy satellites, which dropped film back to Earth. More than 800,000 images were declassified in 1995 and are free from the U.S. Geological Survey.

docs.title: 'Bin Ladin Determined To Strike in US'
docs.summary: A President's Daily Brief item given to President George W. Bush five weeks before the attacks of 11 September 2001. It was declassified for the 9/11 Commission in 2004.
docs.wiki: Bin Ladin Determined To Strike in US

docs.title: Abbottabad compound files
docs.summary: Nearly 470,000 files seized in the raid on Osama bin Laden's house, released by the CIA in November 2017.

docs.title: Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose files
docs.place: National Archives of India, New Delhi
docs.summary: Files on the Indian independence leader and the mystery of his death. The Government of India declassified more than 300 files from 2016.

docs.title: Brazil's military dictatorship records
docs.by: Brazilian military government and U.S. agencies
docs.summary: Records used by Brazil's National Truth Commission, which reported in 2014 on killings and torture under the 1964–1985 regime.

docs.title: Japan's wartime cabinet and army records
docs.summary: Records of Japan's war up to the surrender, digitised and opened online by the Japan Center for Asian Historical Records since 2001.

docs.title: Preliminary Assessment: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena
docs.by: Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI)
docs.summary: A public report on 144 sightings by U.S. military personnel since 2004. Only one was explained; the report found no evidence of foreign or extraterrestrial technology.
